name: Banda-Mbrès
confidence_why: The initial-stress rule rests solely on Toqué's 1904 colonial essay on the Moruba dialect, whose term "accent tonique" Éboué (1918) explicitly glosses as pitch rather than stress for Banda, while the modern descriptions of sister Banda lects (Sampson 1985 for Tangbago, Althabégoïty 2024 for Ngbugu) treat them as three-tone languages with no contrastive word stress, so the record is essentially unconfirmed.

Règle II. — Dans les mots de quatre syllabes, Taccent tonique ^e place sur la première et la troisième syllabe. kôukoudoûnou, placer sous. new_statements.quote: ACCENT. La langue banda est chantée, c'est-à-dire, que chaque syllabe a sa tonalité propre, et est prononcée sur un ton plus élevé ou plus bas que la voisine. On distingue trois tons principaux : le ton haut, [...] le ton moyen, [...] le ton bas [...]. Nous ne noterons ici la tonalité des éléments du langage que dans la mesure où la fonction du mot dans la phrase la fait varier [...] (p. 23) En dehors de l'accent de hauteur, il existe en banda un accent d'intensité qui affecte certaines syllabes des mots, en sorte que les syllabes non accentuées s'abrègent et ont une tendance à disparaître : Bèleda, tronc d'arbre, bleda ; temö, marque du futur, tem ; maræ, faire, mar. (pp. 23-24)
new_statements.translation: ACCENT. The Banda language is sung, that is, each syllable has its own pitch and is pronounced on a higher or lower tone than its neighbour. Three principal tones are distinguished: the high tone, the mid tone, the low tone. We shall mark the pitch of elements here only insofar as the function of the word in the sentence makes it vary. (p. 23) Apart from the pitch accent, there exists in Banda an accent of intensity which affects certain syllables of words, such that the unaccented syllables shorten and tend to disappear: Bèleda 'tree trunk' > bleda; temö, future marker > tem; maræ 'to do' > mar. (pp. 23-24)

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog (Toqué 1904, Morouba dialect) records fixed initial stress in 2-3-syllable words ('accent tonique.. sur la première'). Tisserant 1930 adds the type information the catalog lacks: Banda is a three-tone language in which every syllable has its own tone, and the stress ('accent d'intensité') is a separate phenomenon affecting 'certaines syllabes' with no stated fixed position. Compatible with the existence of word stress, but it does not confirm initial placement, and one of his three examples (Bèleda > bleda, loss of the initial syllable) implies non-initial stress in at least that trisyllable, which sits uneasily with Toqué's Règle I; Toqué's 'accent tonique' may also partly reflect…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Banda is a tone language: every syllable carries its own tone, three level tones (high, mid, low), with tone changes conditioned by syntax (e.g. verb + verbal noun raises the verb vowel's tone, p. 23, p. 83) and the tones alone are beaten on the talking drum (pp. 23-24 n.). Separately from tone ('accent de hauteur') there is an intensity (stress) accent that falls on 'certain syllables' of words; no placement rule is given. Its effect is reduction/loss of unstressed syllables, and the three examples show loss of an initial syllable (Bèleda > bleda) as well as of final syllables (temö > tem, maræ > mar), i.e. the stressed syllable is not always the first.
new_statements.exceptions: none as such; p. 19 notes the vowel œ is 'fréquent en banda, surtout dans des syllabes peu accentuées' (frequent especially in weakly stressed syllables); p. 22 n. 2 notes an optional intercalary vowel in consonant+liquid clusters that is always restored in drum language (kra 'stranger', drummed kara); p. 24 notes loanwords 'reçoivent leurs accents' (receive their tones) like native words.
new_statements.identity_note: Tisserant describes 'la langue banda' as a whole, citing forms by dialect (linda of Bambari and Ippy, banda-banda, togbo, yakpwa, ndokpwa, moruba, and the divergent langwasi, dakpwa, vora); his dialect table (p. 4) lists Moruba ('une partie aux Moroubas (Haute-Ouaka), une autre Nord du Kaga Mbré, Ndellé') and Wada under the 'dialecte banda'. The accent statement (pp. 23-24) is given for Banda generally, not specifically for the Banda-Mbrès cluster (Moruba/Mbré/Buka/Sabanga/Wada); the catalog record (Toqué 1904) is specifically the Morouba dialect.

readall_conflicts: The standing tension recorded in the catalog bundle remains: the catalog stress placement coded per word length as 10 100 1010 (1 = a stressed syllable) rests on Toque 1904 (dialecte Morouba = moru1251), whose 'accent tonique' is contrastive by presence/absence and hedged as 'qui semblent être très générales', while every modern description of a Central Core Banda lect that the earlier passes reached is three-tone with no accent (Cotel 1907 for Togbo, Arom 2007 for Linda, Olson 2001 for Mono), and Sampson 1985 for Tangbago states 'Stress is noncontrastive on the word level; it is governed by tone and word shape'. The two SIL survey reports on Mbre and Moruba already held by the project (Blühberger 2021, JLSR 2021-013 and 2021-031) say nothing about stress or tone. Tisserant 1930 is the one older primary that might decide whether the initial 'accent' of Toque is stress or tone, and it could not be opened. One point of tension, not an outright contradiction: the catalog's only record (Toqué 1904, dialecte Morouba) gives a fixed rule, stress on the first syllable of 2-3-syllable words; Tisserant 1930 (pan-Banda grammar) describes Banda as a tone language (three tones, each syllable with its own tone) and says only that an intensity accent 'affecte certaines syllabes des mots' without locating it, and his example Bèleda > bleda (initial unstressed syllable lost) implies a non-initial stress in a trisyllable, contrary to Toqué's Règle I, while temö > tem and maræ > mar are consis…

audit.recode_to: Downgrade from 'fixed stress placement coded per word length as 10 100 1010 (1 = a stressed syllable) to a tone-language / stress-undescribed (or fixed: initial syllable LOW-CONFIDENCE with caution) entry: caution text 'sole source is a 1904 pre-tonological essay; Banda lects have 3 contrastive level tones (Olson 2001, Althabégoïty 2024); Éboué 1918 equates period 'accent tonique' with pitch; Toqué's accent minimal pairs are probably tonal; only Règle III (final-vowel weakening) is stress-like'. Final choice between 'initial prominence' and 'no word stress' should follow a read of Cloarec-Heiss 1988/1967.
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote verified verbatim at the stated place in the held Toqué 1904 scanned, and the Morouba = Moruba (Banda-Mbrès) identification is supported by Toqué's own Avertissement. (2) The classification rests entirely on a 1904 colonial administrator's ethnographic essay. Every modern description of a Banda lect we hold or downloaded (Olson 2001 Mono; Althabégoïty 2024 Ngbugu) analyses Banda as a three-level tone language and says nothing about word stress; Éboué 1918, writing on Banda among others, explicitly says the 'accent tonique' of these languages is really high/low pitch. Toqué's list of words distinguished by 'absence of accent' (eau/seins, flèches/arachides, compter/corne) is the signature of lexical tone. So a fixed-stress stress placement coded per word length as 10 100 1010 (1 = a stressed syllable) coded from this source, with no caution flag, is at risk of being a tone misreading; only his final-vowel-weakening rule is independent stress-l
